record.original_question: For each n>= 3, is there a square-free word u of length n such that u  beta u is square free for some beta?

evidence.quote: For each n>= 3, is there a square-free word u of length n such that u  beta u is square free for some beta?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $\Sigma^*$ denote the set of finite words over $\Sigma$. A word $w \in \Sigma^*$ is called square-free if it contains no nonempty factor of the form $xx$ (i.e., there are no nonempty $x \in \Sigma^*$ and words $p, q \in \Sigma^*$ with $w = pxxq$). Given two words $u, v \in \Sigma^*$, a shuffle of $u$ and $v$ is any word obtained by interleaving the letters of $u$ and $v$ while preserving the relative order of letters within $u$ and within $v$; equivalently, if $u = u_1 u_2 \cdots u_m$ and $v = v_1 v_2 \cdots v_k$, a shuffle is a word of length $m+k$ whose positions are partitioned into an ordered subsequence equal to $u$ and an ordered subsequence equal to $v$. We denote by $u \shuffle v$ the set of all shuffles of $u$ and $v$, and refer to an element of $u \shuffle u$ as a self-shuffle of $u$.

Determine whether the following holds: for every integer $n \geq 3$, there exists a square-free word $u$ of length $n$ (over some finite alphabet) and a self-shuffle $w \in u \shuffle u$ such that $w$ is square-free.
artifact.status_search_result: The question was resolved affirmatively: for every $n \geq 3$ there exists a square-free ternary word of length $n$ admitting a square-free self-shuffle. This was established in "Square-Free Words with Square-Free Self-Shuffles" published in the Electronic Journal of Combinatorics.

status_evidence.title: Square-Free Words with Square-Free Self-Shuffles
status_evidence.snippet: For every n≥3 there is a square-free ternary word of length n with a square-free self-shuffle.
status_evidence.claim: Affirmative answer to the question for all n≥3.
